title: Count Substrings That Differ by One Character
statement:
Count the pairs `(a, b)` where `a` is a non-empty substring of `s`, `b` is a substring of `t` of the same length, and the two disagree in exactly one position (every other position holds the same letter). Put differently, `a` turns into `b` by changing exactly one of its characters to a different letter.

A substring is a contiguous run of characters, and substrings are told apart by where they sit: the same text taken from two different places in `s` or in `t` gives different pairs. Return the number of such pairs.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters only
notes:
## Intuition

The direct way is to try every substring of `s` against every equally long substring of `t` and count the mismatches, which costs O(n · m · L²). Instead, line the two strings up at every possible shift (`offset = i - j`) and walk along each alignment once. A pair of substrings that ends at aligned positions `(i, j)` has exactly one mismatch precisely when its start lies after the second-to-last mismatch and no later than the last mismatch. So at every position we only need to know how many such starts exist.

## Approach

1. For each `offset` from `1 - t.length` to `s.length - 1`, start at `i = max(offset, 0)` and `j = i - offset`.
2. Walk `i` and `j` forward together. `run` counts the positions since the last mismatch, including the current one.
3. When `s[i] !== t[j]`, set `starts = run` (every start from just after the previous mismatch up to this one) and reset `run` to 0.
4. Add `starts` to `count` at every position: each of those starts gives one substring pair ending here with exactly one mismatch.
5. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aba"`, `t = "baba"`, offsets -3 to 2.

- `offset = -3`: `s[0] = "a"` against `t[3] = "a"`: a match with no mismatch yet, adds 0.
- `offset = -2`: `"ab"` against `t[2..3] = "ba"`: two mismatches; each copies `run = 1` into `starts`, adding 1 + 1 = 2.
- `offset = -1`: `"aba"` against `t[1..3] = "aba"`: all match, adds 0.
- `offset = 0`: `"aba"` against `"bab"`: three mismatches in a row, each with `starts = 1`, adds 3.
- `offset = 1`: `s[1..2] = "ba"` against `"ba"`: all match, adds 0.
- `offset = 2`: `s[2] = "a"` against `t[0] = "b"`: one mismatch, adds 1.

Total `count = 6`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · m): there are `n + m - 1` alignments and each position of each is visited once.
- Space: O(1): only a few counters.

## Pitfalls

- Count positions, not distinct strings: equal substrings at different places are separate pairs.
- Pairs with zero mismatches must not count; before the first mismatch on an alignment `starts` stays 0.
- After a mismatch, `run` restarts at 0 so that the next mismatch only allows starts after this one.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | number of pairs found so far |
| `offset` | shift `i - j` between the aligned positions of `s` and `t` |
| `i`, `j` | current aligned positions in `s` and `t` |
| `run` | positions walked since the last mismatch on this alignment |
| `starts` | how many start points give exactly one mismatch for a pair ending here |

narration.3: Try every way of lining s up against t; offset is i - j.
narration.4: The alignment begins at the first position that exists in both strings.
narration.5: j sits offset places behind i.
narration.6: No mismatch seen yet on this alignment, so no valid start points.
narration.7: Positions walked since the last mismatch.
narration.8: Walk along the alignment until either string ends.
narration.9: Include the current position in the run.
narration.10: A mismatch becomes the single allowed difference for pairs ending from here on.
narration.11: Valid starts run from just after the previous mismatch up to this one.
narration.12: Begin counting again from this mismatch.
narration.14: Each valid start gives one pair that ends at (i, j) with exactly one difference.
narration.19: Every alignment has been walked; return the total.
